Where does most of your ATP actually come from?

blocks.x: Glycolysis gave you a net 2 ATP. The Krebs cycle gave you another 2 ATP. That is four ATP from an entire glucose molecule — nowhere near enough to run a human being. What those pathways really produced was something else: loaded electron carriers, NADH and FADH₂. The electron transport chain (ETC) is where those carriers are finally cashed in, yielding roughly 34 ATP from one glucose.

The whole process runs on one simple physical idea: electrons falling from a high-energy carrier down to oxygen release energy, and that energy is used to pump protons uphill. The protons then flood back through a turbine, and that turbine makes ATP.

Electrons falling downhill are the river. The complexes are the pumps that use that flowing water to push more water up behind a dam. The dam is the proton gradient. ATP synthase is the turbine at the bottom of the dam. Notice what this means: the energy is never handed directly from electrons to ATP — it is stored in the dam first. That indirect step is the single most important idea in this topic.

Two names describe the same overall event: oxidative phosphorylation (ADP is phosphorylated using energy from oxidation) and the respiratory chain. And this is the real answer to a question you have never needed to ask: why do we breathe? Oxygen's job is to sit at the end of this chain and accept the spent electrons.

sections.title: The mitochondrion — form fits function

blocks.x: Every step of the ETC happens inside the mitochondrion, and the organelle's architecture explains the chemistry. It has two membranes, and they could hardly be more different.
The outer membrane is freely permeable to small molecules and ions because it is riddled with porins (a ~10,000 dalton limit). It is a sieve, not a barrier.

The inner membrane is the opposite: protein-rich (about 4:1 protein to lipid) and essentially impermeable. It holds the four respiratory complexes, ATP synthase and the transporters. Its impermeability is not incidental — you cannot hold a proton gradient across a leaky membrane, so this one property makes the entire chapter possible.

The inner membrane is thrown into folds called cristae, which multiply the surface area available for the machinery. Between the two membranes lies the intermembrane space (composition much like cytosol), and inside everything is the matrix — a protein soup (~500 mg/ml) holding the Krebs cycle enzymes, pyruvate dehydrogenase, fatty-acid oxidation enzymes, plus mitochondrial DNA and ribosomes.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — why muscle mitochondria look different

blocks.x: Muscle cells generally have mitochondria packed with far more cristae than liver cells. More cristae means more surface area, which means more respiratory chain per mitochondrion. The tissue that needs sustained ATP builds more assembly line into the same space — the same reason a busy kitchen installs more counters rather than a bigger building.

sections.title: NADH made in the cytosol cannot simply walk in

blocks.x: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol and produces NADH there — but the inner membrane is impermeable to NADH. The electrons must be handed across by a shuttle, and which shuttle is used changes how much ATP you get.

The malate–aspartate shuttle is the efficient one. Cytosolic NADH reduces oxaloacetate to malate, malate crosses into the matrix, and there it hands its electrons to NAD⁺ — regenerating NADH inside the matrix. Because the electrons arrive as NADH, they enter at Complex I and the full proton-pumping route is used (~2.5–3 ATP per pair).

The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle is the cheaper, faster one. It hands electrons to FAD, forming FADH₂, which enters at Complex II — bypassing Complex I entirely. One proton-pumping station is skipped, so the yield drops (~1.5–2 ATP per pair).
An easily-missed point: NADH and FADH₂ are electron carriers, not components of the chain. They deliver electrons and leave. Do not list them as complexes.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — express vs local delivery

blocks.x: Both shuttles deliver the same parcel of electrons to the same factory. The malate–aspartate shuttle drops it at the front gate, so it passes through every workstation. The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle drops it at a side door halfway down the line — faster, but the first workstation never gets to add its value. Less work done means less ATP.

sections.title: Why electrons flow one way and never back

blocks.x: The chain is a series of oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions. Electrons are passed from carrier to carrier, and each carrier is arranged so that the flow is spontaneous.

The property that governs this is <term d="A measure of a molecule's tendency to accept electrons. Strongly negative = eager to donate electrons; strongly positive = eager to accept them.">reduction potential (E°′)</term>:

items: NADH ≈ −0.32 V — strongly negative, so it is a powerful reducing agent, poised to give electrons away.
O₂ ≈ +0.82 V — strongly positive, so it is a powerful oxidising agent, desperate to accept them.

blocks.x: Electrons therefore flow from the most negative carrier to the most positive one, and each successive acceptor has a greater electron affinity than the donor before it. That stepwise arrangement is deliberate: it releases the energy in small, controlled instalments rather than one destructive burst.
The energy released is calculated with:
ΔG°′ = − n F ΔE°′

where n is the number of electrons transferred, F is the Faraday constant (23.04 cal/volt) and ΔE°′ is the difference in standard reduction potentials. A positive ΔE°′ gives a negative ΔG°′ — that is, a spontaneous, energy-releasing step.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a staircase, not a cliff

blocks.x: Burning glucose in open air releases all its energy instantly as heat — useful for a fire, fatal for a cell. The ETC turns that cliff into a staircase. Each step drops the electron a little lower and lets the cell capture the energy released, instead of being cooked by it.

sections.title: Meet the machinery, one station at a time

blocks.x: The chain is built from four membrane-bound multi-protein complexes in the inner membrane, each containing Fe–S centres, haem or copper prosthetic groups. Crucially, only Complexes I, III and IV pump protons. Complex II does not.

Complex I — NADH–CoQ reductase (NADH dehydrogenase). Over 30 subunits, ~850 kD. It takes 2 electrons from NADH and passes them first to FMN. FMNH₂ then converts the 2-electron transfer into 1-electron transfers onward through Fe–S centres to coenzyme Q. Pumps 4 H⁺ per 2 electrons.

Complex II — succinate–CoQ reductase. This is succinate dehydrogenase, the same enzyme you met in the Krebs cycle — the only enzyme that belongs to both. FAD accepts 2 electrons and passes them one at a time via Fe–S proteins to ubiquinone. Pumps no protons, which is exactly why FADH₂ yields less ATP than NADH.

Complex III — CoQ–cytochrome c reductase. Coenzyme Q passes electrons to cytochrome c through a distinctive redox loop called the Q cycle. Pumps 4 H⁺. Cytochromes, like Fe–S clusters, are one-electron transfer agents.

Complex IV — cytochrome c oxidase. The end of the line. It collects electrons from cytochrome c and performs a four-electron reduction of O₂ to form 2 H₂O, using two haems (a and a₃) and two copper centres. Pumps 2 H⁺.

Between the complexes sit two mobile carriers: coenzyme Q (ubiquinone), which is lipid-soluble and moves within the membrane, and cytochrome c, which is water-soluble and moves along the membrane surface.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the assembly line and its couriers

blocks.x: The four complexes are fixed workstations bolted to the factory floor. Coenzyme Q and cytochrome c are the two runners carrying parts between them. Complex II is the side entrance where a second supplier (FADH₂) drops goods straight onto the line — convenient, but that supplier misses the first station's proton-pumping bonus.

sections.title: How the gradient becomes ATP

blocks.x: Electron transport and ATP synthesis are not directly connected. Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory states that they are coupled indirectly, through a proton electrochemical gradient. This won a Nobel Prize and is the conceptual heart of the topic.
It works in two coupled halves:

items: Respiration: spontaneous electron transfer through Complexes I, III and IV drives the non-spontaneous ejection of H⁺ from the matrix. As protons leave, the matrix becomes more alkaline and negatively charged relative to the cytosol — creating both a pH gradient and a membrane potential.
ATP synthesis: the non-spontaneous making of ATP is coupled to the spontaneous return of H⁺ into the matrix through ATP synthase (F₁F₀).

blocks.x: Together the pH and electrical gradients form the proton-motive force. And here is the detail that makes it work: ATP synthase is the only route by which protons can return. Every proton that comes back must pay a toll, and the toll is ATP.

ATP synthase is a mechanical machine: flowing protons turn the F₀ rotor, the rotation drives conformational change in the F₁ head, and that change forces ADP and Pi together. Finally, the ATP made must be exported to the cytosol, while ADP and Pi are brought back in — a continuous exchange.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the turnstile at a stadium

blocks.x: The crowd (protons) has been pushed outside and wants back in. Every gate is locked except one turnstile, and that turnstile is geared to a generator. Nobody gets in without turning it, so every returning person produces electricity. Punch extra holes in the wall and the crowd streams back freely — the generator stops, even though the crowd is still moving. That is exactly what an uncoupler does.

sections.title: What a glucose molecule is actually worth

blocks.x: By convention, 1 NADH ≈ 2.5–3 ATP and 1 FADH₂ ≈ 1.5–2 ATP. The difference is entirely explained by entry point: FADH₂ enters at Complex II and misses Complex I's proton pumping.

Across a whole glucose molecule, roughly 36 ATP are produced under aerobic conditions — with only 4 of those coming from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. The overwhelming majority comes from the ETC.
That contrast is worth naming precisely:

items: Substrate-level phosphorylation: a phosphoryl group is transferred directly from a substrate to ADP or GDP. It happens in glycolysis (cytoplasm) and the Krebs cycle (matrix), and it works with or without oxygen.
Oxidative phosphorylation: ATP is made indirectly, using the proton gradient generated by electron transport. It absolutely requires oxygen.

blocks.x: The overall equation hides all of this: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ~36 ATP. Worth tracing where each piece came from — the CO₂ from oxidised carbons cleaved off sugars, and the water from O₂ after it accepts electrons at Complex IV. Heat is produced too, though the equation never mentions it.

sections.title: Inhibitors, uncouplers and famous poisons

blocks.x: Many of the most lethal poisons known act on this one pathway — which tells you how central it is. They fall into two classes that behave very differently.
1 · Respiration (electron transport) inhibitors block electron flow itself. Oxygen consumption stops, the gradient is never built, and ATP synthesis stops with it.

items: Complex I: rotenone (an insecticide — and used by Amazonian communities to catch fish), amytal/amobarbital, MPP⁺, piericidin.
Complex II: 3-nitropropionate.
Complex III: antimycin A, TTFA, dimercaprol.
Complex IV: cyanide, azide, H₂S and carbon monoxide — these bind tightly to the ferric (Fe³⁺) form of haem a₃.

blocks.x: 2 · Phosphorylation inhibitors block ATP synthase instead: oligomycin and DCCD plug the F₀ proton channel. Atractyloside is different again — it blocks the ATP/ADP antiporter, so ATP cannot leave and ADP cannot enter.

Here is the subtle part worth understanding rather than memorising: an ATP synthase inhibitor also stops electron transport. If protons cannot flow back in, the gradient becomes too steep to pump against, and the chain stalls. This is why coupling must be intact for oligomycin to suppress respiration — whereas cyanide stops oxygen uptake regardless.

3 · Uncouplers are the interesting case: they do not block anything. They are hydrophobic molecules with a dissociable proton that ferry H⁺ back across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. Electron transport continues — in fact it speeds up — oxygen is still consumed, but no ATP is made and the energy is released as heat.

items: 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), dicoumarol, CCCP, salicylate, Ca²⁺.

Thermogenin (UCP1) is the body's own regulated uncoupler, found in the brown adipose tissue of newborns and hibernating mammals. It generates deliberate non-shivering thermogenesis — costly in ATP, but it keeps the animal warm.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the diet drug that killed people

blocks.x: 2,4-dinitrophenol was sold as a weight-loss drug: burn fuel without storing the energy, and the weight falls off. It works exactly as advertised — which is the problem. All that energy leaves as heat, and users ran fevers around 107 °F and died. It was withdrawn. A newborn baby uses the same trick safely, because thermogenin is regulated and DNP is not.

sections.title: Oxygen, inheritance and disease

blocks.x: Everything in this topic converges on one dependency: no oxygen, no ATP.

The role of oxygen. O₂ sits at the end of the chain, accepting electrons and picking up protons to form water. Remove it and the chain backs up — every carrier stays reduced with nowhere to pass electrons, proton pumping stops, the gradient collapses, ATP production ceases, and cells die. That is why suffocation, cyanide poisoning and severe ischaemia kill so quickly, and it is the real reason you breathe.

Other terminal acceptors. Oxygen is the best acceptor but not the only one. Microbes can use NO₃⁻, Mn⁴⁺, Fe³⁺, SO₄²⁻ and CO₂ — this is anaerobic respiration. The energy yield falls in the same order (O₂ ≈ −479 kJ/mol; SO₄²⁻ ≈ −77 kJ/mol), which is why organisms use them in that sequence.
Mitochondrial inheritance. Because mitochondria carry their own DNA and sperm mitochondria are lost at fertilisation, mitochondrial traits are inherited maternally, in a non-Mendelian pattern:

items: All children of an affected mother are affected.
No children of an affected father inherit it.
Both sexes can be affected.

blocks.x: Why the symptoms are neurological and muscular. Mitochondrial genes encode several ETC and oxidative phosphorylation components. Brain and muscle depend most heavily on oxidative phosphorylation, so these diseases present as neuropathies and myopathies.

A pharmacological footnote. Statins have been reported to affect mitochondria in several ways — reducing coenzyme Q10 levels, inhibiting respiratory complexes, and increasing oxidative stress — which is one proposed explanation for statin-associated muscle symptoms.

sections.title: Key takeaways

blocks.x: If you keep only a handful of ideas from this topic, keep these.

items: The ETC does not make ATP directly. It builds a proton gradient; ATP synthase makes the ATP. Coupling is indirect — that is chemiosmotic theory in one line.
Complexes I, III and IV pump protons. Complex II does not. That single fact explains why NADH yields more ATP than FADH₂.
Electrons flow from negative to positive reduction potential, downhill, in controlled steps, ending at O₂.
O₂ is the terminal electron acceptor, and the water you produce comes from it.
Inhibitors stop electron flow; uncouplers let it run but waste the energy as heat. Both stop ATP — by opposite mechanisms.
The inner membrane's impermeability is essential. No sealed membrane, no gradient, no ATP.

blocks.x: And the connection backwards: glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle exist largely to load NADH and FADH₂. This chapter is where all of that finally becomes usable energy.

mnemonics.h: I, III and IV pump — II does not
lines: Only Complexes I, III and IV move protons across the membrane, which is exactly why FADH₂, entering at Complex II, yields less ATP than NADH.
NADH is worth about 2.5 ATP and FADH₂ about 1.5 — the modern figures behind the 30–32 ATP total per glucose.
Rotenone blocks Complex I, Antimycin A blocks III, Cyanide and CO block IV, and Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase — four poisons, four places.
2,4-dinitrophenol and thermogenin let protons leak back without passing through ATP synthase: the chain runs fast, oxygen is used, but heat comes out instead of ATP.
Cytosolic NADH entering by the malate-aspartate shuttle stays NADH; by the glycerol phosphate shuttle it becomes FADH₂ and loses an ATP.
Location: inner mitochondrial membrane, folded into cristae
Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ flow downhill to O₂, the final acceptor
Released energy pumps H+ into the intermembrane space
I · NADH dehydrogenase (FMN, Fe-S) — pumps H+
II · Succinate dehydrogenase (FAD) — pumps none, hence the lower yield
III · Cytochrome bc1 — pumps H+
IV · Cytochrome c oxidase (a, a3, Cu) — pumps H+, reduces O₂ to water
Mobile carriers: coenzyme Q in the lipid, cytochrome c on the outer face
Proton-motive force = pH gradient + membrane potential
ATP synthase (Complex V): F0 channel + F1 catalytic head
NADH ≈ 2.5 ATP · FADH₂ ≈ 1.5 ATP (older texts: 3 and 2)
Total per glucose ≈ 30–32 ATP
Complex I: rotenone, amytal · Complex III: antimycin A
Complex IV: cyanide, carbon monoxide, azide
ATP synthase: oligomycin
Uncouplers: 2,4-dinitrophenol, thermogenin in brown fat — heat, not ATP
Malate-aspartate (liver, heart): cytosolic NADH → mitochondrial NADH
Glycerol phosphate (muscle, brain): NADH → FADH₂, one ATP less

items.d: NADH hands two electrons to FMN, then through Fe-S centres to coenzyme Q. Four protons pumped. Blocked by rotenone and amytal.
The only TCA enzyme in the membrane. Succinate → fumarate passes electrons via FADH₂ to coenzyme Q. No protons pumped, so FADH₂ yields less ATP.
A small lipid-soluble carrier that collects electrons from both Complex I and Complex II and ferries them through the membrane to Complex III.
Passes electrons from QH₂ to cytochrome c through the Q cycle, pumping four protons. Blocked by antimycin A.
A small mobile protein on the outer face of the inner membrane, carrying one electron at a time to Complex IV. Its release into the cytosol triggers apoptosis.
Cytochromes a and a3 with copper centres deliver four electrons to O₂, making two molecules of water, and pump two protons. Blocked by cyanide, CO and azide.
Protons flow back down their gradient through the F0 channel, rotating the F1 head and driving ADP + Pi → ATP. Blocked by oligomycin, bypassed by uncouplers.
